title: Best Insurance Agency Automation Software for Agents
summary: Insurance agency automation software cuts manual work and speeds up operations. Identify which platform offers the features and pricing you need most.
body_markdown:
## 3. Activepieces


If the gap you need to close sits between systems,[Activepieces](https://www.activepieces.com/pricing) connects them through 750 integrations (so there are likely pre-built connectors for what you're already using) under an MIT-licensed core, so you're not locked into proprietary licensing, and you can self-host it or run it in your cloud; **it doesn't replace your agency management system** .


It fits the gaps between systems: a web form, an approval, an email, a payment record. It doesn't hold client records, policies or renewals, so it can't be the system of record.


If your management system already automates the job natively, build it there and keep this for what crosses the boundary.


A larger agency worried that self-hosting means a cut-down product can set that aside: the air-gapped self-hosted build keeps the same enterprise controls as the managed cloud, including single sign-on, role-based permissions, an audit trail of who changed what, and a place to keep secrets.


MoneyGram, Moneypenny, Alan and FundingSocieties run Activepieces in production.


I have no confirmed list price or task allowance for Activepieces to quote here. Read the vendor's pricing page against your own monthly task estimate before choosing cloud over self-hosting.


Self-hosting changes who carries the cost: you pay in maintenance time instead of plan fees, and someone must own that.


### Worked workflow: web quote request to task and email


100 leads received, 30 contacted, 15 quoted and 3 bound: that is the typical agency funnel, according to[Startkadence](https://www.startkadence.com/guides/cost-per-policy-ceilings-lead-source-profitability-modeling) . That means 70 of every 100 leads are never contacted at all, so the first touch is where automation earns its place.


In six steps, the canvas below shows the pattern: a web form collects the request, AI extracts the fields, a person approves, and the flow branches on the decision, so the reader must refer to the visual diagram to understand the full process.


Take from it that the human approval step is built in, not bolted on.


Look at the ends of the canvas: Stripe and Gmail sit there, which shows a document workflow.


For a quote request, keep the first four steps and change the ends: an accepted request creates a task for the producer, and a rejected one sends a polite email, so the quote flow's implementation reduces to customizing the final decision branching.


Neither end needs your management system to expose a connector.


Test three things before you roll out, because they remain unconfirmed:


1. Whether Activepieces has a connector for your management system. I couldn't confirm one, so you may be using a generic web request step or file import.
2. Who edits the flow when a field changes. The canvas is visual, but a producer has to be willing to open it.
3. Whether the approval task suits your team. Run ten real requests through it and see whether anyone looks at the queue, because the 70 uncontacted leads are usually a habit problem, not a tooling one.


Activepieces is the better fit for larger agencies that need to keep automation inside their own network without giving up enterprise controls.


The air-gapped self-hosted build carries the same list as the managed cloud (single sign-on, SCIM, custom role-based permissions, audit logs, release management and secret managers), so choosing full control over where it runs doesn't mean accepting a fraction of the product.


That holds on the criterion of deployment control, and it doesn't change the limits noted above: it connects systems at the boundary and is not a system of record, so where your management system already automates a job natively, build it there.
